This app talks to a MeshCore LoRa radio over Bluetooth or USB. Without one there is nothing to send messages with: there is no internet fallback, by design.
Pair over Bluetooth, or plug one in over USB.
Open Settings → Connection to pair or plug in a radio.
Your name is broadcast in every advert: the whole mesh sees it. Pick something you\'re happy being known by out there.
Every node on a mesh must share the same frequency, bandwidth, spreading factor and coding rate. Mismatched, you\'ll see an empty app rather than an error.
Direct messages are end-to-end encrypted. Channels are only obfuscated (AES-ECB with a 2-byte MAC and a key that never changes), so treat a channel as a room with an unlocked door, not a sealed one.

A channel is a group conversation across the mesh. It is its secret key: everyone with the same key is in the same channel, whatever each of them calls it.
Only people you give the key to can join.
Enter a secret key someone gave you.
Scan a channel or community QR
Join from a code someone shows you.
Channels are obfuscated, not secure (AES-ECB with a 2-byte MAC). Don\'t send anything you couldn\'t bear to be read.
The Public channel uses a key every MeshCore radio knows. Anyone in range can read and post in it.
Hashtag channels are public: anyone can join by entering the same name, because the key is made from the name. Only a–z, 0–9 and hyphens.
A new random key is made on this phone. Only people you give it to can join. Share it afterwards from the channel\'s settings → Share channel QR.
The name can be anything you like: it stays on this phone. Only the secret key must match.
Messaging, routes, favourites and renaming need it in your radio\'s contacts. Add it, and its full sheet opens.

its route hash is shared, so relays can\'t be credited
Removes nodes from the radio\'s contact list when nothing has been heard from them (no advert and no message) for longer than this.
Favourites are never removed, whatever the slider says. Nor is a node that has never been heard from at all, which is what a contact just added from a QR code looks like.
Conversations are kept. A thread with a removed node shows its key instead of its name, and the node comes back on its own if it advertises again.
Enter the room\'s password to read and post. The room decides what it grants and says so when it replies.
The node decides what this password unlocks and says so when it replies. Many nodes accept a blank password for read-only access.
Rooms often keep the default room password, \"%1$s\", unless the owner changed it.
⚠ TCP links are unencrypted and unauthenticated: message text and repeater login passwords cross the network in the clear.
A disabled transport is never started: it never scans, connects or reads data.
Connect to a radio to edit this node\'s identity.
This radio has no position set. It is still on the mesh: adverts just go out without a location.
\"Follow the system\" uses the phone\'s light or dark setting.

Radio figures never change: frequency stays in MHz, signal in dB and pressure in hPa. What a node sent is stored as it was sent; this only changes how it\'s shown, so switching back and forth loses nothing.
Message storage is encrypted (SQLCipher, key sealed in the device keystore).
Map tiles are the app\'s only automatic internet connection.

With tiles off, nodes still plot on a plain background: nothing is fetched, so no third party learns where you\'re looking. Firmware downloads happen only when you ask. Everything else works in airplane mode.
Mute a single conversation from its own menu.
A muted conversation still counts unread messages: muting stops interruptions, it doesn\'t hide that something arrived.
Secrets (passwords, keys, PSKs) are removed before lines are written.
The log is empty. Secrets (passwords, keys, PSKs) are removed before lines land here.

The MeshCore TCP link is UNENCRYPTED and UNAUTHENTICATED.

• Every message you send or receive crosses the network in plain text.
• Repeater and room passwords cross the network in plain text.
• Anyone who can reach the radio's IP and port can control your radio.

Only use TCP to reach a Wi-Fi or Ethernet MeshCore node on a trusted network you control, never over untrusted Wi-Fi or the open internet.

A line means this repeater heard that node\'s advert directly.
It says nothing about the other direction, and nothing about now: the node records a neighbour when a repeater\'s advert arrives at zero hops, and nothing expires it.
Companions, rooms and sensors are never recorded, so a short list is the firmware being narrow, not a fault.
The list is what this repeater says it hears, relayed by that repeater, and the signal figure is its reading at the time.
The key is stored sealed in the device keystore and on the radio.

The code contains the channel\'s secret key. Anyone who scans it can read everything on this channel, including messages sent before they scanned, because the key never changes and the cipher has no forward secrecy.\n\nThere\'s no way to revoke it: undoing a share means changing the key on every device that uses the channel.
Anyone who scans this can read the channel. Show it only to people you mean to give that to.
This node announced %1$s when it was told to update, so it can be identified exactly.
No update-mode address was recorded for this node, so it will be identified by what it advertises, and named before anything is written to it.

A node in update mode is off the mesh and can only be reached over Bluetooth, from within range of it.\n\n\"Restart it\" asks its bootloader to boot the firmware it already has. That works when the transfer never got as far as erasing anything, the usual case for an update that failed early. If the firmware was already erased, it depends on the bootloader: OTAFIX comes back in update mode, ready to be flashed again, but the standard bootloader comes back as a USB drive and stops answering over Bluetooth. On a standard bootloader, don\'t use this on a node whose transfer had started.
Scan with any MeshCore app to add this node as a contact.

Nothing answered. That can mean none are in range, that they answered with a key prefix matching no contact you hold, or that they run firmware without discovery.
Answered within range. These are contacts you already hold whose key matched a responder\'s prefix: a prefix is not proof of identity.

Their direct messages are dropped as they arrive: not stored and hidden, but never written down at all.
Nobody is blocked. Block someone from their contact sheet.
Deletes old messages from this phone only, in every conversation.
Nothing is deleted from anyone else\'s device. Trimming counts by when a message ARRIVED here, not by the time it claims: a sender\'s clock shouldn\'t decide which of your messages survive.
Deletes this phone\'s copy of everything. It does NOT touch the radio: its contact list, channel slots and identity are on the device and stay there.
This deletes, from this phone only:
• The cached contact list and channel names
• Path history and the discovery inbox
• Nicknames, pins, mutes and region labels
• Anything on the radio: contacts, channels and its identity stay
• Messages other people received from you
Your message history can\'t be recovered: the radio doesn\'t keep a copy to re-sync from.
Also forget stored keys and passwords
Channel keys, repeater passwords and the saved identity seed go too. Channels you have no other copy of the key for become unreadable.
Anyone with the channel key can post under any name, including one you recognise.
A channel message carries a name, not a key, so nothing here can be verified. The list is built from the messages this phone kept: it isn\'t a membership list, and it can\'t tell you who anyone is.
No incoming messages kept for this channel yet. Retention settings affect what\'s here.
Every node you talk to must be on these same four values. If they aren\'t, you won\'t see errors: you\'ll see an empty mesh.
This saves the settings on %1$s; they take effect when it reboots. After that, this radio must be on the same settings to reach %1$s again, or it will need physical access.
Repeaters that relay it appear below as their copies reach this radio. Give it a minute: an advert has to travel out and come back.
Connect a radio first: this measures what the mesh does with your transmissions.
That file isn\'t a MeshConnect backup, or it\'s from a newer version.
A backup is an ordinary file. It leaves the keystore and every protection this phone gives it, so what goes in is a decision, not a default.
Always included: your settings, region names and your contact list (names and public keys). That\'s a map of who you talk to, so keep the file somewhere you\'d keep that.
This build has no authenticated cipher available, so an encrypted backup can\'t be written. Settings-only export still works.

These are encrypted with your passphrase and nothing else. Anyone who has the file and guesses the passphrase can read every channel you\'re in and sign in to every repeater you administer. There\'s no recovery if you forget it.
Contains %1$d settings, %2$d contacts, %3$d channels and %4$d regions.
Contains %1$d settings, %2$d contacts, %3$d channels and %4$d regions, plus an encrypted section.
This backup was made on a different radio. Restoring contacts or channels writes them onto the radio connected now.
Writing to the radio can\'t be undone from here.
Connect to a radio to change its pairing PIN.
Nodes without a screen ship with %1$s, which is public.

Until it\'s changed, anyone in Bluetooth range can pair with this radio and read its contacts, messages and settings: the default is the same on every node without a screen, so it\'s documentation, not a secret. The radio can\'t be asked what its PIN is, so this screen can only set a new one, never show the current one.
Clears the PIN: the node goes back to its built-in default
That\'s the factory default: it protects nothing
The radio will drop its stored PIN and go back to its built-in default.
The radio will use %1$s from now on.

• It keeps pairing with the OLD PIN until the node restarts: the firmware picks the active PIN at startup. You'll be offered a reboot.
• This phone is already paired with the OLD PIN, and only Android can drop that pairing ("Forget device" in the system Bluetooth settings, not Remove under saved radios here). Until you do, the phone reconnects on the old pairing and the change looks like it did nothing.
• Every other phone paired with this radio has to do the same.
• Nothing can read the PIN back off the radio. If you forget it, Bluetooth access is gone until you reach the node another way: USB, or a factory reset that takes its identity with it.

Write it down before you continue.

The new PIN is stored, but the radio keeps pairing with the old one until it restarts.\n\nAfter the reboot your phone will still reconnect without asking for the new PIN: Android remembers the old pairing and only Android can drop it. To test the PIN, remove the pairing in the system Bluetooth settings (\"Forget device\"), which is NOT the same as Remove under saved radios here.

Android is holding a pairing made with the OLD PIN, and an app can\'t delete it. Until you do, this phone reconnects without being asked for the new PIN, so the change looks like it did nothing.\n\nIn Bluetooth settings, find this radio and choose \"Forget device\". The next connection will ask for the new PIN.

Off-grid encrypted LoRa messaging for MeshCore radios. No servers, no accounts, no Google Play Services, no analytics, no crash reporting.
MeshConnect is a fork of MeshCore Hardened. Its protocol layer, engine, storage and most screens are their work.
Transports, foreground service and app scaffolding, by the same author
The mesh firmware and protocol this app speaks
Map tiles and firmware downloads are the only internet connections, and both can be avoided.
Messages, contacts and keys live on this phone and the radio. Nothing is uploaded.
Channels are obfuscated, not secure: AES-ECB with a 2-byte MAC, and the key never changes.
Advert signatures are verified before a contact is imported.
Secrets sit in the device keystore and the message database is encrypted.
MeshConnect is an independent project. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by the MeshCore project or the MeshCore Hardened author.
